<reflection>
- The third experiment (high S, low P) successfully narrowed down the field. The top models (M20, M11, M14, M12) all have NLL values around -60, significantly outperforming the rest. 
- We have confirmed that catalyst deactivation is the dominant secondary mechanism. 
- The aim of the previous turn was achieved, but we are now left with a tight cluster of deactivation models. The current challenge is that under standard steady-state conditions, the concentration of the catalyst-substrate complex `[catS]` is proportional to `[S][cat]`. This makes M14 (`catS => inactive`) and M11 (`S + cat => inactive`) kinetically degenerate. Furthermore, we need to clearly separate product-induced deactivation (M12) and spontaneous free catalyst deactivation (M9, M20).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the degeneracy between M11 and M14, we must push the system outside the standard steady-state approximation. By using a low substrate concentration (S=0.5) and the maximum catalyst concentration (cat=0.20), the total catalyst is comparable to the total substrate. This will cause a massive initial binding event that significantly depletes *free* substrate `[S]`. 
- For M14 (`catS => inactive`), deactivation will be strong because `[catS]` is maximized relative to total S.
- For M11 (`S + cat => inactive`), deactivation will be suppressed because free `[S]` is depleted.
Additionally, by introducing a moderate initial product concentration (P=0.3), we can simultaneously test for M12. Because free `[cat]` will still be relatively high (since cat=0.20 and S=0.5, at least 0.15 of cat remains free or becomes free quickly), M12 (`P + cat => inactive`) will exhibit immediate and rapid deactivation from t=0. M9 (`cat => inactive`) will also show rapid deactivation but without the dependence on P, which the global fit will distinguish using data from previous runs. M20 will show the most extreme deactivation as both its pathways (`cat` and `catS`) are highly active in this regime.
</hypothesis>
